strengths: Addresses a timely and important research question about whether generative models for weights achieve true generalization or merely memorize training data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple complementary metrics (weight space L2 distances, decision boundaries, model outputs, intrinsic dimensions) that strengthen conclusions
Rigorous methodology analyzing 4 representative methods across multiple datasets with careful baselines and thorough appendices
Effective visualizations and clear presentation that make findings accessible and convincing (Figures 2-6)
Honest presentation of negative results that will be valuable for the research community in preventing pursuit of unproductive directions
Includes comparative analysis with models trained from scratch and intrinsic dimension analysis showing fundamental differences between weight and image data complexity
Reproducible work with detailed experimental setup and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty and contribution: paper is primarily an evaluation study without proposing new methods or deep theoretical insights to address the identified memorization problem
Narrow scope: only 4 generative methods from 2021-2023 are analyzed, limited to simple classification models (ResNet-18), single domain (image classification), and relatively small datasets

Lacks theoretical analysis: no explanation of why memorization occurs or discussion of fundamental information-theoretic barriers versus surmountable obstacles; intrinsic dimension analysis (Appendix G) is superficial
P-diff's anomalous behavior (better accuracy-novelty tradeoff) is noted but not deeply investigated—why does it differ and can insights be leveraged to improve other methods?
Evaluation metric choices somewhat arbitrary: maximum similarity metric is post-hoc and not sensitivity-tested; different novelty metrics could alter conclusions

Incomplete experimental coverage: no systematic study of dataset size effects on memorization, limited exploration of why proposed mitigation strategies (modeling factors, data augmentation) fail, and missing statistical significance tests
No constructive solutions or concrete directions provided for achieving weight generalization; unclear whether the identified problems are fundamental or addressable
Limited scope reduces generalizability: findings on simple models and curated datasets may not extend to modern large-scale models, neural field models beyond tested architectures, or other domains

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored question about whether generative models for weights generalize or memorize, which is crucial for understanding the practical utility of weight generation methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 representative methods (Hyper-Representations, G.pt, HyperDiffusion, P-diff), multiple datasets (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, STL-10), and various model architectures with well-designed metrics

Multi-faceted analysis including weight space similarity, model behavior comparison, decision boundary visualization, and intrinsic dimensionality analysis that provides convincing evidence of memorization

Strong empirical evidence with effective visualizations (weight heatmaps, PCA plots, decision boundaries, histograms) showing generated weights closely resemble training checkpoints and produce nearly identical model outputs

Systematic investigation of mitigation strategies (reducing epochs, model size, regularization, permutation augmentation) demonstrating that standard approaches cannot effectively address memorization
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, well-articulated research questions, comprehensive appendices, and detailed experimental setup supporting reproducibility
Broader context provided through comparison with image generation models and intrinsic dimensionality analysis that reveals fundamental differences in data structure between weights and images
weaknesses: Limited novelty in proposed solutions - the paper is primarily a diagnostic study documenting what doesn't work without offering constructive solutions or new methods to address memorization

Scope limitations: only 4 generative methods analyzed, relatively small standard datasets (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10), and limited checkpoint training data (e.g., 300 for P-diff), raising questions about generalization to modern large-scale settings

Incomplete mechanistic understanding - while memorization is documented, the fundamental reasons WHY generative models memorize in weight space remain largely unexplored, limiting deeper insights into the problem

P-diff experimental setup differs from other methods (authors train custom model; uses only final 2 batch norm layers), making cross-method comparisons less uniform; P-diff's better trade-off vs. noise is marginal
Limited exploration of what constitutes acceptable accuracy-novelty trade-offs in practice, and unclear which applications genuinely require novel weights versus checkpoint interpolation
Noise addition baseline is somewhat weak; comparison could benefit from stronger baselines or more sophisticated alternatives
Brief and somewhat speculative analysis of why image generation generalizes better than weight generation (Section F) deserves deeper investigation

No clear direction provided for future work - the paper identifies limitations but offers minimal guidance on what approaches might overcome them or why existing paradigms may be fundamentally constrained

strengths: Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation using complementary metrics: L2 distance in weight space, model behavior similarity, non-parametric data-copying detection, and intrinsic dimensionality analysis provide converging evidence for memorization rather than relying on a single metric

Thorough experimental coverage across multiple methods (4 representative approaches), datasets (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, ShapeNet), and systematic ablations examining data scaling, model capacity, training length, and other factors

Important and timely research question that challenges recent claims in the literature about generative models for neural network weights; provides practical value to the community by documenting critical limitations

Well-designed experiments with appropriate baselines (noise addition, interpolation, from-scratch training) and well-executed ablation studies that systematically isolate different causes of memorization

Insightful findings from intrinsic dimensionality analysis (Appendix J) showing weights have higher intrinsic dimensions than images yet generalize worse, suggesting data properties fundamentally differ between modalities
Methodologically sound analysis with statistical significance testing via non-parametric tests, reproducible experimental setups documented in appendices, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper is primarily an empirical critical analysis rather than proposing new methods or theoretical insights; memorization in generative models is established, and applying this to weight generation is relatively straightforward

Weight space comparison limitations not fully addressed: L2 distance is insensitive to permutation symmetries and other structural invariances in weight matrices; while acknowledged, this fundamental limitation deserves more comprehensive treatment and limits the strength of claims

Severely limited exploration of solutions: Section 4.2 on structural priors is underdeveloped with only permutation symmetry experimentally tested; scaling and other symmetries mentioned but not validated; paper identifies problems without proposing concrete methodological fixes

Root causes of memorization remain shallow: limited data and overparameterization are identified but relative contributions not quantified; why some methods memorize more than others is insufficiently investigated; implications of intrinsic dimensionality differences between modalities are underdeveloped

Inconsistent experimental setups across methods: different training configurations, datasets, hyperparameters, and checkpoint set sizes make fair cross-method comparison difficult; some methods had to use different codebases due to missing pre-trained models

Key claims rely on indirect evidence: P-diff memorization claim (Section 3.3) shows generated weights concentrate near training weights but this could indicate structured generalization rather than pure memorization; interpolation analysis is limited
Limited scope of comparisons: image diffusion comparison (Appendix H) has substantial task differences making it an imperfect analogy; only one data-copying detection method employed

Presentation could be improved: dense appendices with 11 sections reduce accessibility; key experiments relegated to supplementary material; intrinsic dimensionality analysis feels somewhat disconnected from main narrative

strengths: Addresses an important research question about whether generative weight models truly generalize or merely memorize training data, with clear practical implications for the field

Comprehensive multi-perspective evaluation using L2 distance, weight heatmaps, decision boundary analysis, similarity metrics, and statistical tests across multiple datasets and four different generative methods
Compelling visualizations (especially Figures 2, 4-6) that effectively demonstrate memorization patterns across different methods and datasets
Systematic investigation of contributing factors (limited data, model capacity, structural priors, weight distributions) with well-designed ablation studies
Thorough experimental methodology with extensive appendices (11 sections) providing reproducibility, additional visualizations, and deeper analyses including intrinsic dimensionality
Well-organized presentation with clear logical flow from motivation through evidence to mechanistic understanding, combined with clear writing and informative figure captions
Appropriate statistical grounding using non-parametric tests and multiple evaluation metrics to quantify memorization
weaknesses: Limited novelty: memorization in generative models with limited data and high capacity is not surprising; the contribution is primarily empirical characterization rather than methodological innovation
Lack of proposed solutions: identifies problems but offers no methods to improve generalization in weight generation, limiting practical impact for practitioners
Unclear practical implications: does not clearly establish when generating novel weights would be beneficial or what the actual value proposition of weight generation is, even if models memorize

Narrow experimental scope: limited to small models on image classification (MNIST, CIFAR-10); unclear whether findings generalize to modern large-scale models, transformers, or other domains like NLP/RL

Insufficient treatment of P-diff: this method shows interpolation rather than memorization but deserves deeper analysis as a potential solution path; the distinction between interpolation and memorization is under-explored

Weight vs. behavioral similarity conflation: does not sufficiently address that two networks with very different weights can have nearly identical behaviors; the connection between L2 distance and behavioral similarity needs more critical analysis
Limited mechanistic depth: while identifying contributing factors, the paper lacks explanation of why these factors lead to memorization or rigorous bounds on model capacity effects

Weak baseline comparisons: lacks comparison with simple baselines (random initialization, classical schemes) and non-generative approaches, limiting context for whether memorization is actually problematic

Intrinsic dimensionality insights relegated to appendix: analysis showing weight data has higher intrinsic dimensionality than images (Appendix J) deserves main paper treatment as it could explain fundamental memorization patterns
Statistical presentation could be stronger: while using ZU test, lacks comprehensive confidence intervals and precise quantitative thresholds for claims like 'closely resembles'
